claim: Lithium was initially reported for treatment as a mood stabilizer over 60 years ago (Cade, 1949).
source: Lithium was initially reported for treatment as a mood stabilizer over 60 years ago (Cade, 1949)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cade, 1949, which is a reference to prior scholarly work.

claim: Lithium is still widely used for the treatment of Bipolar Disorder.
source: Lithium was initially reported for treatment as a mood stabilizer over 60 years ago (Cade, 1949) and is still widely used for the treatment of Bipolar Disorder (Mitchell, 2013; Poolsup et al., 2000; Vieta and Valentí, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mitchell, 2013; Poolsup et al., 2000; Vieta and Valentí, 2013.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying lithium's antimanic and antidepressant responses remain poorly understood.
source: However, despite its extensive use for the treatment of bipolar disorder, the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying its antimanic and antidepressant responses remain poorly understood (Can et al., 2014; Malhi and Outhred, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Can et al., 2014; Malhi and Outhred, 2016.

claim: Putative mechanisms for the therapeutic effects of lithium include inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β).
source: Putative mechanisms for the therapeutic effects of lithium include inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β) (Klein and Melton, 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klein and Melton, 1996.

claim: Putative mechanisms for the therapeutic effects of lithium include upregulation of neurotrophins and their receptors.
source: Putative mechanisms for the therapeutic effects of lithium include inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β) (Klein and Melton, 1996), upregulation of neurotrophins, as well as their receptors, and downregulation of α-amino-3-hydroxyl-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) expression (Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2004, 2010; Gray et al., 2003; Seelan et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010) among others.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Putative mechanisms for the therapeutic effects of lithium include downregulation of AMPAR expression.
source: Putative mechanisms for the therapeutic effects of lithium include inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β) (Klein and Melton, 1996), upregulation of neurotrophins, as well as their receptors, and downregulation of α-amino-3-hydroxyl-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) expression (Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2004, 2010; Gray et al., 2003; Seelan et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010) among others.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2004, 2010; Gray et al., 2003; Seelan et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010.

claim: BDNF and aberrant signaling through TrkB have been proposed to underlie both the pathophysiology and treatment of bipolar disorder.
source: BDNF and aberrant signaling through its high affinity receptor tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) have been proposed to underlie both the pathophysiology and treatment of bipolar disorder (Autry and Monteggia, 2012; Malhi et al., 2013; Scola and Andreazza, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Autry and Monteggia, 2012; Malhi et al., 2013; Scola and Andreazza, 2015.

claim: Patients with bipolar disorder have decreased peripheral BDNF mRNA in blood lymphocytes and monocytes in comparison to healthy controls.
source: Previous work has shown that patients with bipolar disorder have decreased peripheral BDNF mRNA in blood lymphocytes and monocytes in comparison to healthy controls (D'Addario et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to D'Addario et al., 2012.

claim: Both manic and depressive states in patients with bipolar disorder have been associated with significantly decreased BDNF blood serum levels compared to patients in euthymic states and healthy controls.
source: Moreover, both manic and depressive states in patients with bipolar disorder have been associated with significantly decreased BDNF blood serum levels compared to patients in euthymic states and healthy controls (Fernandes et al., 2015; Tunca et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2015; Tunca et al., 2014.

claim: Post-mortem analysis of hippocampal tissue has revealed reduced BDNF protein levels in patients with bipolar disorder.
source: Post-mortem analysis of hippocampal tissue has also revealed reduced BDNF protein levels in patients with bipolar disorder (Knable et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knable et al., 2004.

claim: Experimental interventions that cause manic-like behaviors in rodents have been shown to result in decreased BDNF mRNA and protein levels in the hippocampus.
source: In rodents, experimental interventions that cause manic-like (Frey et al., 2006; Fries et al., 2015; Jornada et al., 2010) and depressive-like behaviors (Smith et al., 1995; Tsankova et al., 2006; Ueyama et al., 1997) have also been shown to result in decreased BDNF mRNA and protein levels in the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Frey et al., 2006; Fries et al., 2015; Jornada et al., 2010.

claim: Experimental interventions that cause depressive-like behaviors in rodents have been shown to result in decreased BDNF mRNA and protein levels in the hippocampus.
source: In rodents, experimental interventions that cause manic-like (Frey et al., 2006; Fries et al., 2015; Jornada et al., 2010) and depressive-like behaviors (Smith et al., 1995; Tsankova et al., 2006; Ueyama et al., 1997) have also been shown to result in decreased BDNF mRNA and protein levels in the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smith et al., 1995; Tsankova et al., 2006; Ueyama et al., 1997.

claim: Lithium treatment is associated with increased BDNF protein levels in the serum of patients with bipolar disorder.
source: In contrast, lithium treatment is associated with increased BDNF protein levels in the serum of patients with bipolar disorder (Cunha et al., 2006; de Sousa et al., 2011; Tramontina et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cunha et al., 2006; de Sousa et al., 2011; Tramontina et al., 2009.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment has been shown to increase BDNF mRNA and protein expression in hippocampus, cortex, and amygdala as well as cortical neurons in culture in rodent models.
source: In rodent models, chronic lithium treatment has been shown to increase BDNF mRNA and protein expression in hippocampus, cortex, and amygdala as well as cortical neurons in culture (Fukumoto et al., 2001; Jornada et al., 2010; Yasuda et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fukumoto et al., 2001; Jornada et al., 2010; Yasuda et al., 2009.

claim: Lithium treatment has been shown to increase TrkB activity in neuronal cultures suggesting an increase in BDNF-TrkB signaling.
source: Lithium treatment has also been shown to increase TrkB activity in neuronal cultures suggesting an increase in BDNF-TrkB signaling (Hashimoto et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hashimoto et al., 2002.

claim: BDNF is necessary for the antidepressant response of conventional antidepressants.
source: While previous work has demonstrated that BDNF is necessary for the antidepressant response of conventional antidepressants (Adachi et al., 2008; Ibarguen-Vargas et al., 2009; Monteggia et al., 2004, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adachi et al., 2008; Ibarguen-Vargas et al., 2009; Monteggia et al., 2004, 2007.

claim: BDNF is necessary for the rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine.
source: While previous work has demonstrated that BDNF is necessary for the antidepressant response of conventional antidepressants (Adachi et al., 2008; Ibarguen-Vargas et al., 2009; Monteggia et al., 2004, 2007), as well as the rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine (Autry et al., 2011; Lepack et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Autry et al., 2011; Lepack et al., 2014.

claim: The lithium protocol resulted in a lithium serum concentration in treated mice that was within the therapeutic range of 0.5–2 mM.
source: This protocol resulted in a lithium serum concentration in treated mice that was within the therapeutic range of 0.5–2 mM (Amdisen, 1980), with an average concentration of 1 mM (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amdisen, 1980 and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lithium protocol resulted in an average lithium serum concentration of 1 mM in treated mice.
source: This protocol resulted in a lithium serum concentration in treated mice that was within the therapeutic range of 0.5–2 mM (Amdisen, 1980), with an average concentration of 1 mM (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Following 11 days of lithium treatment, there was a significant increase in phosphorylation of GSK3β at serine nine relative to total GSK3β.
source: To confirm our lithium protocol produced the expected molecular effects, we examined GSK3 inhibition (Klein and Melton, 1996; Stambolic et al., 1996), by measuring the phosphorylation of GSK3β at serine nine with western blot analysis and found a significant increase relative to total GSK3β (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Klein and Melton, 1996; Stambolic et al., 1996.

claim: Lithium treated mice had a significant increase in Bdnf mRNA expression in the hippocampus.
source: Using Q-PCR targeted to the coding exon of Bdnf, we found lithium treated mice had a significant increase in Bdnf mRNA expression (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Lithium treated mice had a significant increase in BDNF protein expression in the hippocampus.
source: We also found a significant increase in BDNF protein expression (Figure 1E) in lithium treated mice relative to CTL mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Littermate control mice treated with lithium showed a significant reduction in immobility time in the FST compared to control mice that did not receive lithium.
source: Littermate control (CTL) mice treated with lithium showed a significant reduction in immobility time that was suggestive of an antidepressant-like response compared to CTL mice that did not receive lithium (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Loss of Bdnf in the inducible Bdnf KO mice did not alter immobility in the FST compared to control mice.
source: In agreement with previous data we found that loss of Bdnf in the inducible Bdnf KO mice did not alter immobility in the FST compared to CTL mice (Monteggia et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data and a citation to Monteggia et al., 2004.

claim: Bdnf KO mice administered lithium showed a significant reduction in immobility in the FST comparable to KO mice that did not receive lithium.
source: We also found that Bdnf KO mice administered lithium showed a significant reduction in immobility comparable to KO mice that did not receive lithium (Figure 2A) suggesting that BDNF is not necessary for the antidepressant-like effect of lithium in the FST.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BDNF is not necessary for the antidepressant-like effect of lithium in the FST.
source: We also found that Bdnf KO mice administered lithium showed a significant reduction in immobility comparable to KO mice that did not receive lithium (Figure 2A) suggesting that BDNF is not necessary for the antidepressant-like effect of lithium in the FST.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Littermate control mice treated with acute amphetamine have a significant increase in the total number of horizontal beam breaks compared to vehicle treated mice.
source: Littermate CTL mice treated with acute amphetamine have the expected significant increase in the total number of horizontal beam breaks compared to vehicle treated mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Control mice receiving lithium treatment showed a small non-significant increase in the total number of beam breaks compared to vehicle treated control mice.
source: CTL mice receiving lithium treatment showed a small non-significant increase in the total number of beam breaks compared to vehicle treated CTL mice, and were indistinguishable from chronic lithium treated mice receiving acute amphetamine, indicating that lithium treatment could prevent the hyperactivity induced by amphetamine (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lithium treatment could prevent the hyperactivity induced by amphetamine in control mice.
source: CTL mice receiving lithium treatment showed a small non-significant increase in the total number of beam breaks compared to vehicle treated CTL mice, and were indistinguishable from chronic lithium treated mice receiving acute amphetamine, indicating that lithium treatment could prevent the hyperactivity induced by amphetamine (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Inducible Bdnf KO mice receiving acute amphetamine showed a significant increase in the number of beam breaks compared to vehicle treated Bdnf KOs.
source: In contrast, while inducible Bdnf KO mice receiving acute amphetamine showed a significant increase in the number of beam breaks compared to vehicle treated Bdnf KOs, and a slight increase with chronic lithium treatment, the chronic lithium treated Bdnf KO mice receiving acute amphetamine still had a significant increase in the number of beam breaks comparable to amphetamine treatment alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data.

claim: Chronic lithium treated Bdnf KO mice receiving acute amphetamine still had a significant increase in the number of beam breaks comparable to amphetamine treatment alone.
source: In contrast, while inducible Bdnf KO mice receiving acute amphetamine showed a significant increase in the number of beam breaks compared to vehicle treated Bdnf KOs, and a slight increase with chronic lithium treatment, the chronic lithium treated Bdnf KO mice receiving acute amphetamine still had a significant increase in the number of beam breaks comparable to amphetamine treatment alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data.

claim: Lithium treatment does not block the hyperlocomotor effects of amphetamine in inducible Bdnf KO mice.
source: These data demonstrate that lithium treatment does not block the hyperlocomotor effects of amphetamine in inducible Bdnf KO mice and thus suggests that BDNF is required for the antimanic-like effect of lithium.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data.

claim: BDNF is required for the antimanic-like effect of lithium.
source: These data demonstrate that lithium treatment does not block the hyperlocomotor effects of amphetamine in inducible Bdnf KO mice and thus suggests that BDNF is required for the antimanic-like effect of lithium.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data.

claim: In control mice, chronic lithium treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the slope of the I/O curve in hippocampal slices in comparison to mice not treated with lithium.
source: We found that in CTL mice, chronic lithium treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the slope of the I/O curve in hippocampal slices in comparison to mice not treated with lithium (Figure 2C), indicating that chronic lithium treatment reduces hippocampal synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment reduces hippocampal synaptic strength.
source: We found that in CTL mice, chronic lithium treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the slope of the I/O curve in hippocampal slices in comparison to mice not treated with lithium (Figure 2C), indicating that chronic lithium treatment reduces hippocampal synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Inducible Bdnf KO mice that did not receive lithium had a similar slope of the I/O curve compared to untreated littermate control mice.
source: Inducible Bdnf KO mice that did not receive lithium had a similar slope of the I/O curve compared to untreated littermate CTL mice (Figure 2C) showing that the loss of BDNF did not impact synaptic efficacy.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The loss of BDNF did not impact synaptic efficacy.
source: Inducible Bdnf KO mice that did not receive lithium had a similar slope of the I/O curve compared to untreated littermate CTL mice (Figure 2C) showing that the loss of BDNF did not impact synaptic efficacy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The slope of the I/O curve in the hippocampal slices from the inducible Bdnf KO mice treated with lithium was unchanged in comparison to the untreated control and Bdnf KO mice.
source: We also found that the slope of the I/O curve in the hippocampal slices from the inducible Bdnf KO mice treated with lithium was also unchanged in comparison to the untreated CTL and Bdnf KO mice (Figure 2C), suggesting that BDNF expression is required for the lithium-mediated reduction of synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BDNF expression is required for the lithium-mediated reduction of synaptic strength.
source: We also found that the slope of the I/O curve in the hippocampal slices from the inducible Bdnf KO mice treated with lithium was also unchanged in comparison to the untreated CTL and Bdnf KO mice (Figure 2C), suggesting that BDNF expression is required for the lithium-mediated reduction of synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lithium treatment produces a significant decrease in AMPAR miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) amplitudes in cultured neurons.
source: Previous work has shown that lithium treatment produces a significant decrease in AMPAR miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) amplitudes in cultured neurons, which has been suggested to underlie the antimanic effects of lithium (Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010.

claim: Lithium treatment has been suggested to underlie the antimanic effects of lithium through decreased AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes.
source: Previous work has shown that lithium treatment produces a significant decrease in AMPAR miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) amplitudes in cultured neurons, which has been suggested to underlie the antimanic effects of lithium (Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010.

claim: Lithium treatment resulted in a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in comparison to NaCl treated or untreated control neurons.
source: Lithium treatment resulted in a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in comparison to NaCl treated or untreated CTL neurons (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Lithium treatment resulted in a 41% decrease in the slope of rank-ordered AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to untreated neurons.
source: We found that lithium treatment resulted in a 41% and 26% decrease in the slope compared to untreated and NaCl treatment, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lithium treatment resulted in a 26% decrease in the slope of rank-ordered AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to NaCl treatment.
source: We found that lithium treatment resulted in a 41% and 26% decrease in the slope compared to untreated and NaCl treatment, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lithium produces a downward scaling of all AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes and impacts post-synaptic homeostatic plasticity.
source: These data show lithium produces a downward scaling of all AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes and impacts post-synaptic homeostatic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rank-order analysis data.

claim: Lithium did not produce changes in mEPSC frequency compared to untreated or NaCl treated neurons.
source: Notably, lithium did not produce generalized effects on synaptic measures as there were no changes in mEPSC frequency compared to untreated or NaCl treated neurons (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Lithium treatment results in a significant decrease in GluA1 surface expression relative to total GluA1 in comparison to untreated or NaCl treated neurons.
source: We performed surface biotinylation experiments and found lithium treatment results in a significant decrease in GluA1 surface expression relative to total GluA1 in comparison to untreated or NaCl treated neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GFP infected neurons treated with chronic lithium had a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in comparison to untreated or NaCl treated neurons.
source: As expected, GFP infected neurons treated with chronic lithium had a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in comparison to untreated or NaCl treated neurons (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: In BDNF deficient cultures, there was no difference in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to GFP infected neurons.
source: In BDNF deficient cultures, Bdnffl/fl neurons infected with Cre, there was no difference in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to GFP infected neurons suggesting loss of BDNF does not impact this synaptic measure (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Loss of BDNF does not impact AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes.
source: In BDNF deficient cultures, Bdnffl/fl neurons infected with Cre, there was no difference in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to GFP infected neurons suggesting loss of BDNF does not impact this synaptic measure (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment of BDNF deficient cultures induced a small but nonsignificant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes.
source: In contrast to wild-type neurons, we found chronic lithium treatment of BDNF deficient cultures induced a small but nonsignificant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes (Figure 4D) suggesting a requirement for BDNF.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Chronic lithium's effect on AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes is dependent on BDNF.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that chronic lithium's effect on AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes is dependent on BDNF.
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiology data comparing BDNF-deficient and control neurons.

claim: GFP infected neurons treated with lithium had a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitude compared to untreated or NaCl treated neurons.
source: Consistent with our previous results, GFP infected neurons treated with lithium had a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitude compared to untreated or NaCl treated neurons (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Ntrk2 fl/fl neurons infected with CreGFP had indistinguishable AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to GFP infected neurons.
source: We found Ntrk2 fl/fl neurons infected with CreGFP, had indistinguishable AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to GFP infected neurons demonstrating that loss of TrkB does not affect this synaptic measure (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Loss of TrkB does not affect AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes.
source: We found Ntrk2 fl/fl neurons infected with CreGFP, had indistinguishable AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to GFP infected neurons demonstrating that loss of TrkB does not affect this synaptic measure (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Lithium treatment of Ntrk2 deficient neurons did not affect AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes showing a requirement for TrkB in lithium's effect on AMPAR mEPSC responses.
source: In agreement with data from the Bdnf deficient neurons, we found lithium treatment of Ntrk2 deficient neurons did not affect AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes showing a requirement for TrkB in lithium's effect on AMPAR mEPSC responses (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The GFP infected neurons treated with lithium had a significant reduction in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to untreated neurons showing that the loss of Dnm3 does not impact the effect of lithium on synaptic function.
source: The GFP infected neurons treated with lithium had a significant reduction in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes compared to untreated neurons showing that the loss of Dnm3 does not impact the effect of lithium on synaptic function (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Deletion of both Dnm1 and Dnm3 occluded the effect of chronic lithium treatment on AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in comparison to untreated cultures.
source: In contrast, deletion of both Dnm1 and Dnm3 occluded the effect of chronic lithium treatment on AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in comparison to untreated cultures demonstrating that lithium is potentiating dynamin dependent endocytosis of AMPAR (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Lithium is potentiating dynamin dependent endocytosis of AMPAR.
source: In contrast, deletion of both Dnm1 and Dnm3 occluded the effect of chronic lithium treatment on AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in comparison to untreated cultures demonstrating that lithium is potentiating dynamin dependent endocytosis of AMPAR (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment resulted in a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in neurons recorded with vehicle in the pipette solution.
source: Consistent with previous data, chronic lithium treatment resulted in a significant decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in neurons recorded with vehicle in the pipette solution (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: The presence of Dyngo in the pipette solution rescued the decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes seen after lithium treatment.
source: In contrast, the presence of Dyngo in the pipette solution rescued the decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes seen after lithium treatment (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment enhances AMPAR endocytosis to alter synaptic function in a dynamin dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that chronic lithium treatment enhances AMPAR endocytosis to alter synaptic function in a dynamin dependent manner and the loss of dynamin, specifically Dnm1 and Dnm3, can rescue the synaptic deficits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dynamin deletion and inhibition experiments.

claim: The loss of dynamin, specifically Dnm1 and Dnm3, can rescue the synaptic deficits caused by lithium.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that chronic lithium treatment enhances AMPAR endocytosis to alter synaptic function in a dynamin dependent manner and the loss of dynamin, specifically Dnm1 and Dnm3, can rescue the synaptic deficits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dynamin deletion and inhibition experiments.

claim: Lithium requires BDNF-TrkB signaling to mediate its antimanic effects.
source: In the current study, we report that lithium requires BDNF-TrkB signaling to mediate its antimanic as well as synaptic effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral and electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Lithium requires BDNF-TrkB signaling to mediate its synaptic effects.
source: In the current study, we report that lithium requires BDNF-TrkB signaling to mediate its antimanic as well as synaptic effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment in vivo results in a sustained increase in BDNF mRNA and protein expression.
source: Chronic lithium treatment in vivo results in a sustained increase in BDNF mRNA and protein expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR and western blot data.

claim: BDNF is required for the antimanic effects of lithium.
source: However, while BDNF is required for the antimanic effects of lithium it is not required for the antidepressant effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral experiments.

claim: BDNF is not required for the antidepressant effects of lithium.
source: However, while BDNF is required for the antimanic effects of lithium it is not required for the antidepressant effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral experiments.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment in vivo caused a significant decrease in I/O curves from hippocampal slices that were dependent on BDNF expression.
source: We determined that chronic lithium treatment in vivo caused a significant decrease in I/O curves from hippocampal slices that were dependent on BDNF expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal slices.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment results in a significant synaptic downscaling of AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes that was dependent on BDNF as well as its high affinity receptor, TrkB.
source: We investigated the effect of chronic lithium on synaptic function and found a significant synaptic downscaling of AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes that was dependent on BDNF as well as its high affinity receptor, TrkB.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from cultured neurons.

claim: The decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes was due to a decrease in postsynaptic surface expression of GluA1 driven by dynamin-dependent AMPAR endocytosis.
source: The decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes was due to a decrease in postsynaptic surface expression of GluA1 driven by dynamin-dependent AMPAR endocytosis, which could be acutely countered by administration of a dynamin inhibitor.
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation and electrophysiology data.

claim: The decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes could be acutely countered by administration of a dynamin inhibitor.
source: The decrease in AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes was due to a decrease in postsynaptic surface expression of GluA1 driven by dynamin-dependent AMPAR endocytosis, which could be acutely countered by administration of a dynamin inhibitor.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data with Dyngo.

claim: Lithium can target AMPA receptor endocytosis to alter synaptic function.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that lithium can target AMPA receptor endocytosis to alter synaptic function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined electrophysiology and biochemistry data.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment in rodents causes a sustained increase in BDNF mRNA and protein in the hippocampus.
source: We show that chronic lithium treatment in rodents causes a sustained increase in BDNF mRNA and protein in the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR and western blot data.

claim: BDNF is required for the antidepressant effects of traditional antidepressants.
source: Previous studies have shown that BDNF is required for the antidepressant effects of traditional antidepressants (Adachi et al., 2008; Monteggia et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adachi et al., 2008; Monteggia et al., 2004.

claim: BDNF is required for the rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine.
source: Previous studies have shown that BDNF is required for the antidepressant effects of traditional antidepressants (Adachi et al., 2008; Monteggia et al., 2004), as well as rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine (Autry et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Autry et al., 2011.

claim: The rapid antidepressant action of ketamine requires BDNF and is protein translation dependent, with BDNF protein rapidly increased but then returning to baseline.
source: The rapid antidepressant action of ketamine requires BDNF and is protein translation dependent, with BDNF protein rapidly increased but then returning to baseline (Autry et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Autry et al., 2011.

claim: Acute manipulation of BDNF protein expression is involved in rapid antidepressant effects while a more chronic increase in BDNF expression is required for antimanic effects.
source: Taken together, these may data suggest acute manipulation of BDNF protein expression is involved in rapid antidepressant effects while a more chronic increase in BDNF expression is required for antimanic effects.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the comparison of lithium and ketamine effects.

claim: Lithium application significantly decreases AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in cultured neurons.
source: Previous work has consistently shown that lithium application significantly decreases AMPAR mEPSC amplitudes in cultured neurons (Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2004; Gray et al., 2003; Seelan et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ankolekar and Sikdar, 2015; Du et al., 2004; Gray et al., 2003; Seelan et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010.

claim: Lithium treatment did not alter AMPA mEPSC frequency demonstrating specificity to the impact of the drug on synaptic transmission.
source: We also found that lithium treatment did not alter AMPA mEPSC frequency demonstrating specificity to the impact of the drug on synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Lithium produced a significant downward multiplicative synaptic scaling of all AMPAR-mEPSC amplitudes consistent with an impact on post-synaptic homeostatic plasticity.
source: Further analysis revealed that lithium produced a significant downward multiplicative synaptic scaling of all AMPAR-mEPSC amplitudes consistent with an impact on post-synaptic homeostatic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rank-order analysis of mEPSC amplitudes.

claim: Lithium decreases GluA1 and GluA2 surface expression in the hippocampus and in cultured cortical neurons.
source: Previous in vivo and in vitro studies have shown that lithium decreases GluA1 and GluA2 surface expression in the hippocampus and in cultured cortical neurons (Du et al., 2003, 2008; Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2003, 2008; Wei et al., 2010.

claim: In vivo lithium treatment caused a significant decrease in I/O curves in hippocampal slices.
source: In addition, we found that in vivo lithium treatment caused a significant decrease in I/O curves in hippocampal slices, which is reminiscent of the decreased AMPA/NMDA ratio previously seen in rats following chronic lithium treatment (Du et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data and a citation to Du et al., 2008.

claim: Chronic lithium treatment in rats causes a decreased AMPA/NMDA ratio.
